body.heading: Charge the balloon
paragraphs: Ask your adult to blow up and tie a balloon. Rub it quickly on a woollen jumper or on clean, dry hair, about ten times.
Rubbing gives the balloon an invisible electric charge called static. You cannot see it, but you are about to see what it can do.

body.heading: Paper jumping beans
paragraphs: Hold the balloon just above tiny bits of tissue paper. The paper leaps up and sticks to the balloon as if it were alive.
The charge pulls the light paper towards it. Static electricity is a real force — the same force that makes lightning, in a tiny, safe size.

body.heading: Hair-raising fun
paragraphs: Hold the charged balloon near your head. Your hair stands up and reaches for the balloon, strand by strand.
On dry days, you might feel tiny static crackles when you take off a jumper. Now you know what that is.

takeaway: Rubbing a balloon gives it a static charge that can pull paper and lift hair like invisible fingers.
safetyNotes: An adult should inflate and tie the balloon. Keep balloons away from very young children, and tidy up any popped balloon pieces straight away, as they are a choking hazard.
screenFreeExtension: Charge the balloon and hold it near a family member's hair to give them a mad scientist hairstyle.
